title: Knight against pawn
summary: Where the knight stops the pawn, why the edge is its enemy, how to face two pawns, how the king helps, and when the knight still mates.
part.front.title: In front of the pawn
part.front.summary: The knight on the promotion square, or watching it, stops even a pawn on the seventh.
part.side.title: From the side, with the fork
part.side.summary: When the front is blocked, the knight watches from the side with a fork ready, as in Kosteniuk against Polgar.
part.knightPawn.title: The knight's pawn
part.knightPawn.summary: Near the edge the knight has fewer squares: the right path exists, and sometimes it starts backwards.
part.rookPawn.title: The rook's pawn
part.rookPawn.summary: The knight's worst enemy: with the pawn on the sixth it still holds, with the check that gains the tempo.
part.king.title: The king helps, and the knight gives itself up
part.king.summary: The knight gains time for the king to arrive; when needed it gives itself up, and the black king loses the tempo.
part.mate.title: When the knight wins
part.mate.summary: Nogueiras against Gongora and Stamma's mate: the king trapped in the corner, in front of its own rook's pawn.
part.recap.title: Summary and practical challenge
part.recap.summary: Three rules for your games, one last position, and an ending to hold in the practical challenge.
step.t_front: The black pawn is on the seventh, one step from queening, and the white king is far away. Can the knight hold the pawn on its own? Where must it stand?
step.t_front.hint1: Which squares can the knight on b2 reach in one move?
step.t_front.hint2: The safest square to stop a pawn is the square where it wants to queen.
step.frontWhy: 1.Nd1. The knight sits on the promotion square and the pawn is stuck. The black king can attack the knight, but it does not have to stay there: from f2, e3, b2 or c3 it still watches d1, and it often comes back with check. Against a central or bishop's pawn, the knight has squares on both sides for this.
step.d_front: Watch the knight hold the pawn with no help at all while the white king comes closer.
step.d_front.m1: 1.Nd1. In front of the pawn, on the promotion square.
step.d_front.m2: 1...Kc2. The black king attacks the knight on d1.
step.d_front.m3: 2.Nf2. The knight leaves, but from f2 it still watches d1.
step.d_front.m4: 2...Kc3. Black tries to get closer from the other side.
step.d_front.m5: 3.Kb6. The white king is coming, in no hurry: the knight handles it alone.
step.d_front.m6: 3...Kd4. The black king goes after the knight.
step.d_front.m7: 4.Kb5. One more king step; the knight keeps guard alone.
step.d_front.m9: 5.Nd1+. The knight returns to the promotion square with check: it gained the tempo, and the pawn cannot move. If the king attacks it again, it goes to b2, on the other side of the pawn, and keeps watching d1.
step.frontMove: Your turn. The pawn is on the seventh. Bring the knight to a square that watches the promotion square, then onto the square in front of the pawn.
step.frontMove.hint: The pawn queens on d1. Find the square from which the knight sees d1 without being captured by the king.
step.frontMove.done: That is it. With 1.Nc3 the knight watched d1, and after 1...Kd3, 2.Nd1 sat right on it. The pawn cannot move.
step.t_side: The black king is on c1, in front of its own pawn: the knight cannot sit on the promotion square. Can White still draw? With which move?
step.t_side.hint1: If the pawn queens, the knight may still have a fork: a check that hits the king and the new queen at the same time.
step.t_side.hint2: First the black king must leave c1. Then find the square from which the knight watches c2 and b3.
step.sideWhy: 1.Ne2+ drives the king off c1, and after 1...Kd2, 2.Nd4 puts the knight to the side. From d4 it watches c2 and b3. If the pawn queens on c1, 3.Nb3+ checks the king and attacks the queen: a fork. If the king steps aside, the knight captures the pawn. This is called lateral control. But 1.Nd3+?, watching from behind, loses: from behind there is no fork, and the black king escorts the pawn.
step.d_side: Watch lateral control work to the end.
step.d_side.m1: 1.Ne2+. The black king must leave the square in front of the pawn.
step.d_side.m2: 1...Kd2, protecting the pawn and attacking the knight.
step.d_side.m3: 2.Nd4. From the side: it watches c2 and b3.
step.d_side.m4: 2...c1=Q. Black queens anyway, to see whether the fork is there.
step.d_side.m5: 3.Nb3+. Check, and the queen on c1 is attacked: a fork. The king steps out of check, and 4.Nxc1 captures the queen. Draw.
step.t_averbakh: Now it is a knight's pawn, and the white king is far away. Does the knight on f5 arrive in time? By which path?
step.t_averbakh.hint1: Near the edge the knight has fewer squares. Think about where it can watch b1 without being driven away.
step.t_averbakh.hint2: From the a-file the knight sees b1. Count the moves to get there.
step.averbakhWhy: The position is Averbakh's. Only 1.Nd6 draws: the knight goes to b5 and a3, and from a3 it watches b1. When the black king attacks, the knight jumps to b1, in front of the pawn, and comes back to a3 with check. The path matters: any other move arrives one tempo late.
step.d_averbakh: Watch the knight arrive in time, without a single move to spare.
step.d_averbakh.m1: 1.Nd6. It looks far from b1, but from d6 the knight reaches b5 and a3 in two jumps.
step.d_averbakh.m2: 1...b3. The pawn runs; it needs two more moves to queen.
step.d_averbakh.m3: 2.Nb5. Now a3 is one jump away.
step.d_averbakh.m4: 2...b2. Now one move is left to queen, and the knight does not watch b1 yet.
step.d_averbakh.m5: 3.Na3. Just in time: from a3 the knight watches b1.
step.d_averbakh.m6: 3...Kc3. The king wants to drive the knight away.
step.d_averbakh.m7: 4.Nb1+. The knight sits on the promotion square with check; when the king attacks it, it goes back to a3, also with check. Draw.
step.t_rook: A rook's pawn on the sixth, and the white king far away. Where must the knight go, and with which move does it start?
step.t_rook.hint1: The knight can only reach the rook's pawn from one side. The good squares are the ones that watch h2.
step.t_rook.hint2: The direct path is one move short. Look for a move the black king cannot ignore.
step.rookWhy: The rook's pawn is the knight's worst enemy: the knight can only come from one side, and in the corner it has very few squares. But with the pawn on the sixth it still works. The idea is to watch h2, from g4 or f1, or to sit on h2. 1.Ne3+ gains the tempo, and 2.Ng4 is already on the right square. Note that the target is h2, not h1: from the corner the knight has almost no way out.
step.d_rook: Watch the check gain the tempo and the knight reach h2.
step.d_rook.m1: 1.Ne3+. The check forces the king to respond, and the knight gains the move it needs to reach g4.
step.d_rook.m2: 1...Ke2. The black king heads toward the pawn.
step.d_rook.m3: 2.Ng4. From g4 the knight watches h2.
step.d_rook.m4: 2...Kf3. The king attacks the knight on g4.
step.d_rook.m5: 3.Nh2+. The knight sits in front of the pawn with check. If the king attacks it again, it goes back to g4 or to f1, always watching h2. Draw.
step.t_king: So far the knight held on its own. Now the h-pawn is on the seventh, and the knight on g3 looks lost. The black king has just gone to d4: on e3 or d2 it would walk into the check from f1, which hits the king and the pawn at the same time. The white king is far away, on b7. How does White draw?
step.t_king.hint1: Count the moves: how many does the black king need to capture the knight, and how many does the white king need to get near the corner?
step.t_king.hint2: Even if the knight falls, the white king on f2 traps the black king in the corner.
step.kingWhy: Dvoretsky's position. 1.Kc6! The white king runs toward f2, and the knight stays where it is until it is attacked; then it goes to h1, in front of the pawn. The black king spends moves capturing it, and each of its moves is a move for the white king. When the black king captures on h1, the white king reaches f2, and Black has no move: stalemate. A draw, even without the knight.
step.d_king: Watch the race of the kings.
step.d_king.m1: 1.Kc6. The white king runs to the centre, heading for f2.
step.d_king.m2: 1...Ke5. The black king goes after the knight.
step.d_king.m3: 2.Kc5. The knight does not need to move yet.
step.d_king.m4: 2...Kf4. It attacks the knight on g3.
step.d_king.m5: 3.Nh1. The knight goes into the corner, in front of the pawn.
step.d_king.m6: 3...Kf3. The black king gets close to the corner.
step.d_king.m7: 4.Kd4. Each move of the black king is a move for the white king.
step.d_king.m8: 4...Kg2. It attacks the knight on h1.
step.d_king.m9: 5.Ke3. The white king is one step from f2.
step.d_king.m10: 5...Kxh1. It captures the knight, but walks into the corner, behind its own pawn.
step.d_king.m11: 6.Kf2. Black has no move: stalemate. Draw.
step.stammaWhy: 81.Kc2! The white king takes b1, b2 and b3, and the black king only has a1 and a2. When the pawn goes to a2, the king on a1 has no squares, and a knight check is mate. The pawn that should have saved Black becomes the wall of its own king. This is Stamma's mate, named after the master from Aleppo who published a chess book in 1737.
step.stammaMove: Now the position that bears Stamma's name. Deliver the mate yourself.
step.stammaMove.hint: A check sends the king to a1; then a waiting move by the king forces the pawn to move.
step.stammaMove.done: Mate! 1.Nb4+ Ka1 2.Kc1 a2 3.Nc2#. The pawn on a2 took the last square from its own king.
step.recap: Three rules. First: the knight stops the pawn in front of it, on the promotion square, or from the side, with the fork ready; not from behind. Second: near the edge, count the moves; the right path may start with a check or with a retreat. Third: against two pawns, capture the one that leaves the knight watching the other, or split the work with the king.
step.recapEdge: And the edge: against a rook's pawn, the knight must arrive while the pawn is still on the sixth, gaining the tempo with a check if needed. The king helps even from far away, and sometimes the knight gives itself up so the king can arrive. And with the king trapped in front of its own rook's pawn, it is the knight that wins.
step.finish: Now the practical challenge. Check, lateral control, and never lose sight of the pawn.
ex.e09: White to move and draw. The black king is in the corner and the g-pawn is running. King and knight together.
ex.e09.hint: The knight goes into the pawn's path; the white king takes squares from the black king, and the checks gain the time.
ex.e09.solution: 1.Nd6 g3, 2.Kf8, close to the black king, g2, 3.Nf7+ Kh7, 4.Ng5+ and then 5.Nf3 or 5.Nh3, watching g1. The checks gave the time that was missing. 1.Kf8 first also draws. A position by Hanneman, via perdomod's collection.
ex.e10: White to move and win. The knight is far away, but the black king cannot leave the corner. Which way does the knight come?
ex.e10.hint: The knight has to reach b4 or c1, the mating squares. It comes through the centre.
ex.e10.solution: 1.Nf5! and 2.Nd4: the knight comes through the centre towards the mating squares, while the black king can only shuffle in the corner. Other moves miss the right timing for Stamma's mate.
key.front: The pawn is one step from promoting and the white king is far away. Even so, the knight on its own watches the promotion square and draws.
key.side: The knight arrives from the side, with check, on a square from which it threatens a fork if the pawn promotes. Only this route draws; checking from behind loses.
key.averbakh: Knight pawn: near the edge the knight has fewer squares, and only one route arrives in time. With it, White draws.
key.rookPawn: Rook pawn: the edge takes squares away from the knight, and nearly everything loses. Only one check brings the knight to watch the square in front of the pawn.
key.grigoriev: Rook pawn and the white king far away: the knight needs one exact check to arrive in time, and then it draws.
key.dvoretsky: The king helps: while the knight holds the pawn, the white king comes closer and shuts the black king in the corner. Draw.
key.stamma: Stamma's mate: the black king is trapped in the corner by its own pawn, and king and knight deliver mate. White wins, whoever moves.
key.nogueiras: Nogueiras against Gongora, Cuban championship, 2001. On move 75, Gongora gave up his knight for White's f6 pawn, counting on capturing White's last pawn afterwards and drawing. He captured it, but his king was left trapped in the corner, in front of its own pawn, and on move 84, facing Stamma's mate, he resigned.
history: Knight against pawn is the ending where a knight has to stop a pawn racing to promote. Most of the time it manages, but it has an enemy: the edge of the board. Near it the knight has few squares, and a rook pawn or knight pawn can get away. It looks simple and isn't: often only one knight route draws, and everything else loses. The classic positions carry the names of the Soviet masters who studied them, such as Grigoriev, Averbakh and Dvoretsky. And there's an old surprise: with the black king trapped in the corner by its own pawn, king and knight can mate. It's Stamma's mate, named after Philipp Stamma, born in Aleppo, Syria, who published it in a book in 1737. In 2001, at the Cuban championship, Gongora gave up his knight for a pawn on move 75 and then captured Nogueiras's last pawn, thinking it was a draw; on move 84, with his king trapped in the corner and that very mate unstoppable, he resigned.
practice: Now the real ending: your knight against a c-pawn on the seventh, with the black king close by. Check, lateral control, fork. Choose your time control and hold the draw.
ex.e11: White to move and draw. The b-pawn is two squares from queening and the knight is far away, on d7. Which way does it arrive in time?
ex.e11.hint: Look for a square from which the knight watches b2 and which the black king cannot take or box in at once.
ex.e11.solution: 1.Nb6! Kd3, 2.Na4! and the knight watches b2. After 2...Kc4, 3.Nb2+, and the knight keeps circling between a4, b2, d1 and d3, always eyeing the square in front of the pawn. The first two moves are the only ones. It is the same right-square idea against the knight's pawn, on other squares. A position by I. Rabinovich, via perdomod's collection.
ex.e12: White to move and draw. Two connected black pawns against the knight, and the black king is already in the corner. Which pawn does the knight let go?
ex.e12.hint: Take a pawn in such a way that, from the square where the knight lands, it watches the other pawn's queening square.
ex.e12.solution: 1.Nf4! g2, 2.Nxh3: the knight captures the h-pawn and from h3 watches g1. 2...Kh2, 3.Kf2!, and the g-pawn cannot move. If 3...Kxh3, 4.Kg1: after 4...Kg3 White has no move, stalemate; after any other king move, 5.Kxg2. A draw either way. The first three moves are the only ones: chasing the g-pawn loses. A study by M. Liburkin, Izvestia, 1932, via Bijbrengen's collection.
ex.e13: White to move and draw. A study by N. Grigoriev, 1932. The h-pawn is still at home, but the knight is in the opposite corner of the board.
ex.e13.hint: The knight must reach g4 or f1 before the pawn reaches the seventh. Count the tempi and look for the route that ends with a check.
ex.e13.solution: 1.Nb4! h5, 2.Nc6! Ke4, 3.Na5!! Kf3, 4.Nc4 h4, and we reach the lesson's Grigoriev position, with the pawn on the fifth: 5.Ne5+! Kg3, 6.Nc4, and from here 7.Ne3 and 8.Nf1 watch h2. The route through a5 looks odd, but it is the only one that brings the knight to e5 with check at the right moment. Almost every move is the only one; only on the fourth does 4.Nc6 also work. A study by N. Grigoriev, Izvestia, 1932, via Bijbrengen's collection.
ex.e14: White to move and draw. A study by N. Grigoriev, 1938. The white king is far away and the b-pawn needs only three moves.
ex.e14.hint: A check to start. After that, sometimes the way to the front of the pawn goes backwards.
ex.e14.solution: 1.Nc7+! Kc4, 2.Ne8!! Kd3, 3.Nd6, and the knight catches the pawn: 3...Kc3 4.Ne4+ Kd3 5.Nc5+ Kd4 6.Nb3+ Kc3 7.Na5 b3 8.Nxb3. The retreat to e8 is the only move: from there the knight goes to d6, where it can jump to b5, c4 or e4. On the third move, 3.Nc7 also works. A study by N. Grigoriev, 1938, via Bijbrengen's collection.
ex.e15: White to move and draw. A study by D. Gurgenidze, 1970. The knight is stuck on h7 and there are two black pawns, far apart.
ex.e15.hint: Split the work: the king takes care of one pawn; the knight, gaining time with a check, of the other.
ex.e15.solution: 1.Ka3! Kf7, 2.Kb4 Kg6, 3.Nf8+! Kf5, 4.Nd7 h5, 5.Nc5 Kg4, 6.Kxb5: the king has the b-pawn, and the knight, which left the corner with check, is already on its way to the h-pawn (7.Ne6, 8.Ng5, 9.Nh3). Up to 5.Nc5 every White move is the only one. A study by D. Gurgenidze, 64, 1970, via Bijbrengen's collection.
ex.e16: White to move and draw. A study by N. Grigoriev, 1932. The knight is in the corner and the white king is far from the h-pawn.
ex.e16.hint: The knight alone cannot stop this pawn. Its job is to gain time for the white king, even by giving itself up.
ex.e16.solution: 1.Nf7! Kd4, 2.Ng5 Ke3, 3.Kd6 Kf4, 4.Nh3+! Kg3, 5.Ng1 Kg2, 6.Ne2!! Kf3, 7.Ke5! Kxe2, 8.Kf4, and the white king arrives in time: 8...Kf2 9.Kg4 h3 10.Kxh3. The knight gave itself up to pull the black king out of the way. 1.Nf7, 4.Nh3+ and 6.Ne2 are the only moves; on the last one, 7.Ng1+ also works. A study by N. Grigoriev, 64, 1932, via Bijbrengen's collection.
part.twoPawns.title: Two pawns
part.twoPawns.summary: Connected pawns: capture the one that leaves the knight watching the other. Split pawns: the king takes one, the knight the other.
step.kostPolgar: The same fork decided a game of Alexandra Kosteniuk, then women's world champion, against Judit Polgar, at the World Blitz Championship in Moscow, 2009. At the end of a knight ending, Polgar checked with 76...Ne6+, Kosteniuk captured the knight with 77.Nxe6, and the black pawn ran: 77...e2. The knight on e6 cannot reach e1, but it can attack the pawn from the side and leave a fork ready for when it queens.
step.kpgMove: Your turn to play like Kosteniuk, on move 78. Stop the e-pawn and let your h-pawn queen.
step.kpgMove.hint: Find the square from which the knight attacks e2 and, if the pawn queens, gives a check to the king on f2 that also hits e1.
step.kpgMove.done: 78.Nf4! The knight attacks e2 from the side. If 78...e1=Q, 79.Nd3+ is a fork: 79...Ke2 80.Nxe1, and the queen falls. The h-pawn queens, and Kosteniuk won the game.
step.retreatWhy: Another knight's pawn, now on the other side, and the pawn on g4 already attacks the knight on h3. Going forward does not work: 1.Nf2? and 1.Nf4? lose the knight to the king on e3, and 1.Ng1? is driven away at once by 1...Kf2. Sometimes the path to the square in front of the pawn starts backwards.
step.retreatMove: Your turn. Save the knight without losing sight of the pawn, and bring it in front of it.
step.retreatMove.hint: Retreat to a square from which the knight can come back to h3 right after the pawn goes past.
step.retreatMove.done: 1.Ng5! The knight retreated, and after 1...g3 it came back with 2.Nh3, eyeing g1. When the pawn went to g2, 3.Ng1 sat in front of it. To get in front, the knight went around behind the pawn.
step.grigorievWhy: Now a position by Grigoriev, with the pawn still on the fifth. The knight on c4 wants to reach g4 or f1, but by the direct path it is one move short: the black king on f3 guards e3 and g4, and the pawn moves first. The way out is to get the black king out of the way first, even if the knight then goes back to c4.
step.grigMove.hint: Start with a check, even if the knight then goes back to c4.
step.grigMove.done: 1.Ne5+! Kg3 2.Nc4. The knight came back, but the black king left f3 and no longer guards e3. After 2...h3, 3.Ne3 h2 4.Nf1+ catches the pawn.
step.t_two: Now there are two connected black pawns, and the knight on d5 can capture either one. The white king is far away and cannot help. Which pawn does the knight capture?
step.t_two.hint1: One of the pawns protects the other.
step.t_two.hint2: After the capture, the knight must watch the square in front of the remaining pawn.
step.twoWhy: 1.Nxb4! The knight captures the pawn that protected the other, and from b4 it watches c2, the square in front of the c-pawn. But 1.Nxc3? loses: after 1...bxc3 the knight is gone, and the new pawn on c3 runs alone.
step.d_two: Watch the two moves that are enough.
step.d_two.m1: 1.Nxb4. It captures and lands on a square that eyes c2.
step.d_two.m2: 1...c2. The pawn tries to get through c2 anyway.
step.d_two.m3: 2.Nxc2+. It captures with check. King and knight against king: draw.
step.twoApart: Now the pawns are far apart. Split the work: the white king, on a1, takes care of the b-pawn; the knight goes after the h-pawn. It cannot reach h1 or h2 in one move, so it needs a square from which, if the pawn advances, a check gains the tempo.
step.twoMove: Your turn: the knight stops the h-pawn, the king the b-pawn.
step.twoMove.hint: The knight does not have to arrive before the pawn: it is enough to have a check ready that gains the tempo when the pawn goes to h2.
step.twoMove.done: 1.Ne3! h2 2.Nf1+ Kf2 3.Nxh2. The h-pawn fell, and after 3...b3, 4.Kb2 stops the b-pawn. Each piece took care of its own pawn.
step.sacWhy: Now the white king is far from the a-pawn, and the black king is close to it. The pawn wants to run down through a3, and the white king wants to reach b2, in front of it, but in a race of kings it arrives one move late. The knight can give the king that move, even by giving itself up.
step.sacMove: Your turn: give the white king the move it is missing.
step.sacMove.hint: Put the knight where it stops the pawn and the black king has to spend a move capturing it.
step.sacMove.done: 1.Nc4! From c4 the knight watches a3 and b2. The black king captured it, 1...Kxc4, but spent the move: 2.Kd1 a3 3.Kc1 a2 4.Kb2, and the pawn does not get through.
step.t_nogueiras: Nogueiras against Gongora, Cuban Championship, Las Tunas, 2001. Gongora gave up his knight for the f-pawn with 75...Nxf6?? He was counting on capturing White's last pawn, on a2, and drawing. He captured it with 80...Kxa2, and the black king ended up in the corner, in front of its own pawn. King and knight against king and pawn is almost always a draw. How does White win here?
step.t_nogueiras.hint1: The black king is in the corner, and the pawn on a3 takes a square away from it.
step.t_nogueiras.hint2: First the white king traps the black king; the knight comes afterwards.
step.d_nogueiras.m1: 81.Kc2. The white king traps the black king on the a-file.
step.d_nogueiras.m2: 81...Ka1. The only move: the king has no other square, and the pawn is blocked by its own king.
step.d_nogueiras.m3: 82.Nc5. The knight comes; if 82...a2, 83.Nb3 is mate.
step.d_nogueiras.m4: 82...Ka2. The king leaves the corner, and the knight needs another route.
step.d_nogueiras.m5: 83.Nd3. From d3 the knight goes to c1 or b4, and Black can only move the king.
step.d_nogueiras.m6: 83...Ka1. The only square again: the king goes back to the corner, where the knight is waiting.
step.d_nogueiras.m7: 84.Nc1. Now the knight takes a2 from the king, and Black only has 84...a2, which runs into 85.Nb3, mate. Gongora resigned.
step.recapMove: One last position before the challenge. The pawn is on the seventh, and the black king on e2 attacks the knight on f3. Use the check and the fork.
step.recapMove.hint: Start with a check that puts the knight on watch over b3 and c2.
step.recapMove.done: Well done. 1.Nd4+ and 2.Nb3+ set up the fork, and 3.Nc1 sat on the promotion square. The pawn does not get through.
